case_info.explanation: The clinical and radiological findings were consistent with POLR3A-related spastic ataxia and exome sequencing revealed a compound heterozygousPOLR3Amutation (c.2000T>A [p.Leu667*]/c.1909 + 22G>A). The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. In summary, POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is a not-so-rare autosomal recessively inherited disease with spastic/ataxic gait and hypodontia as the main clinical features. Cases carrying c.1909 + 22G>A demonstrate spinal cord atrophy and hyperintensities along the superior cerebellar peduncles instead of diffuse leukodystrophy.

The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. case_info.explanation: The clinical and radiological findings were consistent with POLR3A-related spastic ataxia and exome sequencing revealed a compound heterozygousPOLR3Amutation (c.2000T>A [p.Leu667*]/c.1909 + 22G>A). The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. In summary, POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is a not-so-rare autosomal recessively inherited disease with spastic/ataxic gait and hypodontia as the main clinical features. Cases carrying c.1909 + 22G>A demonstrate spinal cord atrophy and hyperintensities along the superior cerebellar peduncles instead of diffuse leukodystrophy.
